title: 3.1 · Sort it out (Organize data)
name: Sort it out (Organize data)
summary: Students learn that real data is messy and must be cleaned before it is charted. In Data Detective's Clean-Up Crew they fix typos, merge repeated rows and remove impossible values, then turn counts into percentages before comparing groups of different sizes. One device per student.
iCan: clean a messy data set: fix typos, merge repeated rows and remove impossible values
turn counts into percentages before comparing groups of different sizes
say what the clean data showed and why
materials: Human Bar Chart cards (one fruit card per student plus three messy cards, for the twin or the block day)
doNow: Most common shoe color in this room: how could we find out fast? Name one thing that could make the count wrong.
plan: Explore: a messy pet survey, chart it, clean it, chart it again

warmup.why: first lesson of the unit: the unit opener, the vocabulary item and today's three exit items as a pre-test; nobody is expected to know them yet, so say so before you start

do: Open Data Detective at Clean-Up Crew on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Case 1 is a pet survey with a row that says twelvety pets and three spellings of dog. Read the question out loud: what is the most common pet?
Chart it as it is first: dog splits into three short bars. Then fix the spellings, merge the repeated row and remove the impossible one. Chart it again and pin the claim.
say: Real data is messy. People make typos, answer twice or write a number that cannot be true.
Clean first, then chart. And never remove a row just because you do not like its answer.
ask: Which rows should we fix, which should we merge and which should we remove? How do you know?
explore.afterAsk: Take three answers. Name the three moves on the board: a typo gets fixed, a repeat gets merged, an impossible value gets removed. Point at the clean chart: one tall dog bar where the messy one had three short ones.
explore.bigIdea: Clean the data first, or the chart tells the wrong story.

play.stretch: the chapter, then 3 stars: the star goes to students who never remove a good row
play.solo: one device per student; a neighbor may read the question out loud, never touch your screen
lookFors: removing every odd-looking row, including true answers that are just unusual
comparing raw counts between two classes of different sizes instead of percentages
merging rows that only look alike: two students with the same answer are not a repeat
play.misconception: Cleaning is not deleting what you do not like: fix typos, merge true repeats, remove only values that cannot be true, and compare groups of different sizes by percent, not by count.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: What would have gone wrong if we kept the messy rows? Show me a case where the messy chart told the wrong story.
One class has 20 students and another has 30. Why compare percentages instead of counts?
showMe: One student shows case 4 on the projector, the messy chart first and the clean one second; the class says what changed.

exit.sentencePrompt: Pick one case you cleaned today. What did the clean data show, and what did you fix to make it show?

rubric.line: Cleaning data: what was fixed and how it changed the result
levels: Names one fix: a typo, a repeat or an impossible value
Names a fix and says how it changed the chart or the claim
Also says why counts became percentages, or why an unusual but true row stays

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: cases 1-3 glow the rows that need a fix
a printed Fix / Merge / Remove card on every desk
hint 1 asks: could this value be true?
stretch: 3 stars on every case: no good row removed
case 6 compares two classes of different sizes; students write the percent claim on paper before they pin it

unpluggedTwin.title: Human Bar Chart, messy edition
materials: one fruit card per student (four fruits)
three messy cards: a misspelled fruit, an impossible count, a second card for one student
masking tape or chalk for a baseline
steps: Every student gets a fruit card; hand the three messy cards to three volunteers as well. Ask: which fruit is the most popular in our class?
Group: students line up behind the sign for their fruit on the baseline. The messy cards make a fifth line and a doubled student.
Clean: the class decides for each messy card whether to fix it, merge it or remove it, and says why. Line up again.
Percent: tell the class another class of 20 had 10 apples. Work out what percent of our class chose apples and compare fairly.
Share: what would the chart have said if we kept the messy cards? Write the clean claim on the board.

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: most common shoe color in this room, how could we find out fast, and what could make the count wrong?

Play Data Detective, chapter Clean-Up Crew, on your own for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 4 2 0 0. Goal: 4 cases. No warm-up and no projector needed; playing signed out is fine.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: What would have gone wrong if we kept the messy rows? Show me a case where the messy chart told the wrong story.
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut

add: the Human Bar Chart twin (15 minutes) before Play
the 3-star stretch and case 6 after Play
10 minutes of chapter Model Makers (quest code 5 2 0 0) as a preview for students who finish

notes: The charts in the game are bars with the numbers printed on them, so they read fine on a washed-out projector and with a screen reader.
The warm-up is a pre-test for unit 3: nobody is expected to know the answers yet. Say so before you start.
Vocabulary beyond the five on the learn card: sort, group.
Most students reach case 4 or 5 of 6 in 18 minutes: that is success.
One device per student at this band.
